subject: Chemistry
title: Brownian Motion: Proof Atoms Exist
description: Learn Brownian Motion: Proof Atoms Exist in one minute.

hook.text: In 1827, Robert Brown watched pollen grains jiggle in water. He couldn't explain why—but Einstein could.

buildup.text: Brown saw tiny pollen particles moving randomly in water under a microscope. No force seemed to push them.

discovery.text: In 1905, Einstein proved the jiggling was caused by invisible water molecules bombarding the pollen from all sides.

twist.text: Many scientists still doubted atoms existed in 1905. Einstein's math showed the jiggle matched atomic theory perfectly.

climax.text: Jean Perrin confirmed Einstein's predictions experimentally in 1908—and won the Nobel Prize for proving atoms are real.

punchline.text: Pollen jiggles, math explains why. Invisible molecules pushing visible grains.

quiz.question: How did Einstein explain Brownian motion?
options: Invisible water molecules randomly bombard visible particles from all sides
Tiny electrical charges in water repel the pollen
Heat convection currents in the water push particles around

details.summary: In 1827 Robert Brown observed pollen grains jittering randomly in water. Einstein mathematically explained this motion in 1905 as the result of invisible molecular collisions, and Jean Perrin's experiments confirmed it, providing the first direct physical proof that atoms exist.
details.whyItMatters: Brownian motion settled the centuries-long debate about whether atoms were real or merely useful fictions. It converted skeptics and established the atomic hypothesis as scientific fact.
takeaways: Brown saw random jittering of particles suspended in liquid
Einstein's 1905 paper explained it as molecular bombardment
Perrin's experiments confirmed Einstein's predictions and proved atoms

faq.question: Why did scientists doubt atoms existed before Brownian motion proof?
faq.answer: Many prominent scientists, including Ernst Mach and Wilhelm Ostwald, argued that atoms were convenient mathematical fictions since no one had directly observed them. They preferred thermodynamic descriptions that did not require assuming invisible particles.

faq.question: How did Einstein's Brownian motion paper differ from his other 1905 works?
faq.answer: Einstein's Brownian motion paper was more practical than his relativity or photoelectric papers. It provided quantitative predictions that could be tested with a microscope, making it uniquely verifiable and ultimately the paper that convinced the last atomic skeptics.
